Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I remind myself it could have been worse
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding triggers are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another in a car accident, given the rest of the profile centers on crash-related and guilt/shame themes. This trigger introduces a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Feelings' is internally incoherent as worded: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of avoidance. Within the maladaptive strategies node, it directly conflicts with an avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' fits poorly with the rest of the profile for a perpetration-type accident trauma in which the patient's appraisals otherwise center on guilt, humiliation, and shattered beliefs. There are no memory, trigger, or strategy items suggesting bodily injury, panic/somatic threat, or physical incapacity to support this appraisal.

vignette: Sunit had always considered himself a meticulous individual, particularly in his role as a tax inspector. His life was methodical and orderly, until one fateful day when he accidentally caused serious injury to another person while driving home from work. The incident occurred on a dark winter evening; the roads were slick with ice, and despite being cautious, Sunit's car skidded off the road, colliding with a pedestrian crossing the street. The immediate aftermath was chaotic and overwhelming. He felt an intense sense of guilt and panic as he watched the injured person being loaded into an ambulance. The memory of sirens wailing in the background and the sound of paramedics calling out instructions still echoed in his mind whenever he thought about that night. Since then, Sunit had been plagued by intrusive memories and vivid imagery associated with car accidents and funerals. The crash itself was a constant source of distress for him. Every time he passed an accident scene or even saw images on the news, it triggered a flood of emotions and flashbacks. He found himself hyper-vigilant while driving, often feeling anxious about making another mistake that could cause harm. His workplace, where cars were frequently in view, became particularly triggering. Sunit's marriage had also been affected by his trauma. His wife noticed the changes in him but didn't fully understand what he was going through. He began avoiding conversations about the incident and even refrained from discussing any topic remotely related to accidents or injuries. This avoidance led to a growing distance between them, as he struggled with the idea that talking about it would only bring back painful memories. He had come to believe that he deserved to suffer because of what happened, an internal punishment that he inflicted upon himself regularly. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, sometimes reminding himself that it could have been worse, which offered a temporary reprieve from his guilt but did little to alleviate his overall distress. The memory of the event was fragmented and inconsistent. Sunit felt like he only remembered parts of what happened, with significant gaps in his recollection. Some moments were crystal clear-the sound of metal scraping against metal, the screams of bystanders-but other details remained a complete blank. This disjointed recollection made him feel even more unsettled, as if pieces of his own memory were missing. His negative appraisals had deeply impacted how he viewed himself and the world around him. Sunit felt permanently humiliated by what happened; it was like a dark cloud hanging over everything he did. His beliefs about how the world should function-safe, predictable, and controllable-were shattered beyond repair. He blamed himself for failing to protect others, which only intensified his feelings of inadequacy and worthlessness. Sunit's work as a tax inspector became increasingly difficult due to these symptoms. He found it hard to concentrate on tasks that required attention to detail, often zoning out in the middle of an audit or report. His supervisors noticed the decline in his performance but were unable to pinpoint the cause. The combination of occupational and relational challenges eventually forced Sunit to seek help. What finally brought him to therapy was a growing sense that he could no longer manage on his own. He felt isolated, both at work and at home, and feared losing everything-the trust of his colleagues, the support of his family, and most importantly, his self-respect. While he was terrified of reliving the trauma through therapy, he also hoped for a chance to regain some semblance of normalcy in his life. Sunit's journey towards recovery began with acknowledging that he needed help to navigate the complex web of guilt, shame, and fear that had engulfed him since that fateful night. He was most afraid of being trapped forever in the shadow of what happened but also most hopeful for a future where he could live without constant reminders of his past mistakes.
